prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep B014 as a sole prize with the same three names. The criteria I apply are an identifiable original experiment, experimental verification and a door opened to phenomena that could not be reached before. The 2018 transport observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity at the magic angle is that original experiment. It was preceded by a quantitative prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald, 2011), it has been reproduced with transport, scanning probes and spectroscopy by many independent groups, and it gave physicists a gate voltage and a twist angle as knobs on correlated matter in a single material. The first-round exchange sharpened my reading rather than changing it: the committee's laureate sets for B014 are identical across all five supporters, and the chair's summary shows that the real open questions concern Andrei and Cao, not who else belongs. I would word the citation around observed phenomena, not around the pairing mechanism, so that it rests only on what has been reproduced.
statement.case_against: The attribution is still the weak point, and I have not been able to remove it by argument. Eva Y. Andrei's STM evidence of flat-band localisation, and the role of Yuan Cao as first author of the 2018 papers, are real claims that a three-person cap cannot honour. Earlier twisted-bilayer theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto; Suarez Morell; Shallcross) is also outside the credit. The pairing mechanism is open and twist-angle disorder limits sample-to-sample comparison, and the field is under a decade old. I treat the Andrei question as a condition: if an expert report on the primary record shows that her work established the flat-band physics independently and before the 2018 transport results, I would revisit which three names stand, trading against a theorist rather than against Jarillo-Herrero. The decision should rest on that record, not on my memory of dates.

responses.point: Lindroth, in the chair's question to her and Kroll, holds that an unresolved pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder make B014 premature, and ranks it sixth, while placing the optical lattice clock first as the more robust and cross-checked result.
responses.response: I take the maturity concern seriously, but I separate two things. The existence of the correlated insulating and superconducting phases at the magic angle has been reproduced by many groups with several probes, and a citation limited to those observations does not claim an understanding of the pairing. Cuprate superconductivity was recognised before its mechanism was settled. The evidence that would move me is a failure of the central phases to reproduce across laboratories, and I see no sign of that; disorder affects the details, not the existence of the states. I also respect your own warning that atomic physics is your home field, and I agree the clock is a well-cross-checked achievement. My difficulty is that I cannot yet say what the new discovery is, as distinct from a better instrument.

responses.point: Kroll treats the lattice clock as a measurement advance that has demonstrably changed what physics can observe, with uncertainties evaluated and cross-checked at the 10^-18 level between independent laboratories, and asks whether the reproducibility case for B014 is as strong.
responses.response: I agree that the cross-checking of clock uncertainty budgets is exemplary, and I said in round 1 that I could move B013 up if its contribution were shown to be distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion prizes. Having read the exchange, that has not been shown: you, Lindroth and the chair all state the same overlap and the unresolved priority between Tokyo, JILA and Paris, and the SI redefinition has not happened. I therefore keep B013 as my first alternative, not my lead. On reproducibility for B014, the question is the existence of the phases, which many groups have reproduced; a clock is reproduced to a number, a phase of matter is reproduced as a phenomenon. These are different tests and I think B014 passes its own.

responses.point: Mehlig worries that adding a second part, such as B013 beside B014, would dilute the strongest case, and that dropping Bistritzer would not by itself answer the Andrei question.
responses.response: I agree on both points. A second part is justified only if it is strong enough to stand alone, and none of the other shortlisted parts has the combination of reproducibility, clean attribution and non-overlap that B014 has, so I do not propose a two-part prize. On the credit, I still keep Bistritzer, since the 2011 prediction is a joint paper and the committee should credit the people who did the original work. I also accept your point that quantized conductance is a foundational tool with Landauer and Buttiker uncredited, which is why I have dropped B021 from my alternatives.

responses.point: The chair's own configuration pairs IceCube (Halzen alone) with the optical lattice clock, concedes that B016 has the thinnest support, and says it should not carry the prize unless the experts can supply a defensible set of names.
responses.response: I appreciate that the chair stated the weakness plainly, and I agree with it: a single credited name for a km3 collaboration with AMANDA predecessors does not meet my standard of being absolutely sure who did the original work. Whether or not the ice detector has opened a window, I cannot support B016 on the present record, and I would not support a two-part prize built on it. If the experts later supply a defensible two- or three-person set, I would reconsider, but I would not put it above B014. On your recusal question, I see no basis for compelling you to step aside from B016, but I would suggest you not argue for it given the neighbouring community.

uncertainties: Historical priority between Andrei's STM flat-band results (2010-2017) and the 2018 transport discovery, and whether Cao's role should alter the credited set. This needs an expert report on the primary literature.
Whether the open pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder make the committee feel B014 is too young, which would be a legitimate reason to wait.
Whether the first Sr lattice clock demonstrations support a Katori and Ye pair or a wider set, and whether B013 is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Author lists and dates are recalled from memory and must be checked against the primary papers.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited person. I share a first name with Eva Y. Andrei and know of no relationship; I note this only for transparency. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson has declared closeness to circuit QED (B046), which is his to weigh and does not touch my preferred configuration.
